title: You are that: the four great sayings
hook: a father hides salt in water and tells his son: you are that
carry: your self is not apart from brahman
tomorrow: the gods turn down a cow and a horse. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed moksha is god's gift, not a city's with the Rig Veda: the real is one, the wise name it many ways. Today a new part begins: the great sayings.

A young man comes home after twelve years of study, a little proud of himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks a strange favor: put this salt in water, and bring it back in the morning. By morning the salt has vanished. Taste it from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the bottom? Salty. It's there, though you can't see it, he says. That fine essence is the self of everything. And you are that.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS.` → `SALT IN THE WATER.` → `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi, you are that, from the Chandogya Upanishad, is one of four very short lines that tradition gathers from four Upanishads and calls the mahavakyas, the great sayings. The others: prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman, from the Aitareya. Aham brahmasmi, I am Brahman, from the Brihadaranyaka. Ayam atma brahma, this self is Brahman, from the Mandukya. Listen to the grammar: consciousness, I, you, this self. Four doors to one Hindu teaching: the atman, your deepest self, is not apart from Brahman, the one reality. How is it read? In Advaita, Shankara's school, the self and Brahman are not two. For Ramanuja, the self is real and distinct, and Brahman dwells within it as its inner ruler, never apart. This lesson doesn't choose. Many teachers hear the same idea in an everyday greeting: namaste, a bow to the one in front of you, read as honoring the divine in them. Now a neighbor. The Buddha's Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Both send the seeker inward. The honest difference: the Buddha's teaching declines to name a lasting self, and doesn't point to Brahman. The great sayings name both.
screen: `FOUR SAYINGS, FOUR HOMES.` · `ATMAN, NOT APART FROM BRAHMAN.` · `NOT TWO, OR AN INNER RULER.` · then, large: `BOTH SEND YOU INWARD.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, if that's comfortable. Let one of the four sayings rest in the mind, whichever comes: you are that, or I am Brahman. Don't work it out. Let it sit like a stone in clear water, and notice the quiet knowing that notices it.
The four mahavakyas: four great sayings from four Upanishads, starting with prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman.
Keep this: your self is not apart from Brahman. Four great sayings, one old teaching. The great sayings, begun.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers in the Vedanta schools study the four great sayings closely; Advaita reads them as pointing to the non-difference of self and Brahman, while Vishishtadvaita reads them as Brahman dwelling in the self as its inner ruler.

mahavakyas.meaning: the great sayings, four short lines from the Upanishads

Aitareya.meaning: the Upanishad that gives prajnanam brahma

Ramanuja.meaning: a Vedanta teacher: Brahman as the self's inner ruler

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

Uddalaka.meaning: a teacher in the Chandogya Upanishad

notes: First day of the part 'The great sayings' (block 1735–1743, so '1 of 9'). Each saying has come up before on this path (Mandukya 254, Chandogya 304/349, Brihadaranyaka 313, Aitareya 404, Panchadashi 1685); this day sets them side by side. Day 1737 opens the Aitareya's 'who is this one?'; this day and 1736 stay out of that passage.
Confirm the verse references: Aitareya 3.1.3 (or 3.3 in some numberings), Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10, Chandogya 6.8.7, Mandukya 2.
Ramanuja's reading (Brahman as inner ruler of a real, distinct self) is given in broad strokes; confirm it is fair to Sri Vaishnava teaching.

Unity thread (wisdom day): the neighbor tradition is Buddhism, in its own words: Dhammapada 1, Max Müller 1881 ('All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.'); confirm the exact Müller wording. Shared: both send the seeker inward, to the mind. Honest difference: the Buddha's teaching (anatta) declines to name a lasting self and does not point to Brahman; the great sayings name both. A Buddhist reviewer should confirm the difference is fair and ranks no one.
